episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, May eighteenth, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Leading off today's Innovation Pulse, artificial intelligence has crossed a historic threshold. OpenAI's GPT-4.5 was judged to be human seventy-three percent of the time in controlled Turing test experiments, a UC San Diego study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found. The actual humans in the same experiments were judged to be human only fifty-four percent of the time. The study is the first to rigorously test large language models using the framework that British mathematician Alan Turing created in nineteen fifty. The test requires a human interrogator to chat simultaneously with two parties, one human and one machine, and then determine which is which. Across randomized experiments with UC San Diego undergraduates and online participants, GPT-4.5 fooled interrogators nearly three-quarters of the time. Meta's LLaMa-3.1-405B was judged human fifty-six percent of the time, a rate statistically indistinguishable from real humans in the experiments. Older systems like ELIZA and GPT-4o scored between twenty-one and twenty-three percent. Cameron Jones, the study's corresponding author, said that with the right prompts, advanced LLMs can exhibit the same tone, directness, humor, and fallibility as humans. The key factor was persona prompting. Without those explicit instructions, GPT-4.5's success rate dropped from seventy-three to thirty-six percent. Study co-author Ben Bergen noted that the models won by making mistakes, using humor, and displaying social traits rather than by demonstrating superior knowledge. Jones said people should be much less confident that they know they're talking to a human when interacting with strangers online today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers today, A.T. and T. cannot find enough workers who know electricity and photonics to install and maintain the fiber optic networks carrying data across the country. CEO John Stankey told CNBC this week that the company needs electricians and fiber optic technicians for infrastructure that A.I. cannot install or maintain itself. Quote, it's not like growing them on trees in the United States, Stankey said. CNBC reported that entry-level hiring at the telecommunications giant has slowed for college graduates in marketing, legal services, accounting, human resources, and IT departments. Ford and other large employers are making the same shift toward skilled trades workers. On job platform Handshake, postings seeking electricians and technicians have increased while postings for entry-level corporate roles requiring four-year degrees have declined markedly. The shifts represent a reversal from decades of corporate hiring patterns that favored four-year college graduates over workers with vocational training.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Meanwhile at UC Berkeley, students earned thirty percent more A grades in courses with writing and coding assignments after ChatGPT launched compared to students in the same courses before the tool became available. Researcher Igor Chirikov analyzed more than three hundred courses across eighty-four departments from twenty eighteen through twenty twenty-five, examining more than five hundred thousand student enrollments. The grade increases were largest in courses where homework counted more heavily toward the final grade. Chirikov found that A.I. primarily converted A-minus and B-plus grades into A grades. The analysis showed that struggling students did not improve their performance. Quote, the results suggest that students have relied on generative A.I. to do better in their studies, not that these classes of students are learning more, Chirikov said. Employers responded to the grade inflation by increasing GPA requirements. On Handshake, the share of job postings requiring a three point five GPA or higher jumped from nine percent in twenty twenty to twenty-five percent in twenty twenty-six.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And in a development affecting academic integrity policies, A.I. detection tools flagged human-written student work as machine-generated while missing actual A.I.-generated text in controlled testing, a CNET investigation this month found. The pattern of accuracy problems has prompted institutions to reconsider their verification methods. CNET found the tools analyze statistical patterns that overlap significantly between human and machine writing. The scores cannot be independently verified or reproduced by different evaluators testing the same text. Students at multiple institutions faced misconduct charges based on incorrect detection scores. The students who challenged the accusations presented drafts, notes, and revision history demonstrating their writing process over time. All of the appeals were successful. In CNET's controlled comparisons, human evaluators who had studied common A.I. writing patterns identified machine-generated text more consistently than the automated systems did. Several institutions have now stopped using detection software as primary evidence in academic integrity cases as generative A.I. tools spread across campuses.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: A.I. Can Now Pass the Turing Test
leadStory.summary: OpenAI's GPT-4.5 was judged to be human seventy-three percent of the time in controlled Turing test experiments, a UC San Diego study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found. The actual humans in the same experiments were judged to be human only fifty-four percent of the time.
